paragraphs.text: The craftsman of the world adorned the heaven with sun and moon and stars, crowned the earth with flowers and plants, and decorated the whole creation in all its variety. We, then, as we take up the account of creation, must marvel at the things that were made and worship the craftsman. These things were not written only so that we might learn that they came to be, but so that we might also marvel at the one who made them. We have said that on the first day he brought forth the materials of created things, and on the second how he made the firmament solid out of the thin nature of the waters, which is why it was called the firmament. For this reason too Christ gathered together the whole inhabited world, which had grown thin and slack, scattered among the various materials of polytheistic error, and made it one faith. And the apostle calls it a firmament, saying: “according to the firmness of your faith in Christ.” So the abyss was divided: the water that stayed below was an abyss, and the water lifted up above was an abyss. How do we know this? David says: “Deep calls to deep at the voice of your cataracts.” So the abyss was divided and the firmament came to be. After that the earth was still covered with water. “And God said,” Scripture says, “Let the water under the heaven be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear.”

The wretched children of the heretics want to know everything and search out the manner of an incomprehensible nature. Since that is so, let them tell us how the water was gathered and where it was gathered, or where it went once it was gathered. After all, as you say, one must not simply follow the words but investigate the realities. God said: “Let the water be gathered.” Where was it gathered? Into the sea. But was the sea not already full then? The earth was full, so surely the sea was too. Where, then, was it gathered? Those who cannot grasp what lies at their feet and before their eyes busy themselves with an unsearchable depth and the incomprehensible abyss of the Godhead. The sea is incomprehensible too, yet it does not shame them out of prying into the craftsman. So let the prophet speak to the heretics as well: “Let the heretics be ashamed,” said the sea, just as he said: “Be ashamed, O Sidon,” said the sea. Hear, then, where the waters were gathered. When God made the earth, the hollows among the mountains did not yet exist. But as soon as he said, “Let the water be gathered,” the earth burst open and formed basins. The facts themselves bear witness that it is the earth that was split apart: there are the islands, and the mountains between. That is why God left the islands and the mountains, so that you might learn that from the beginning the land was joined together. It was the word of God that broke it apart. “Let the water be gathered,” and the earth was laid bare. You should also know that God did not make what we now call the earth as “earth,” nor did he give it that name. From the beginning, at the making of the world, its name was “the dry land,” as David says: “For the sea is his, and he made it, and his hands formed the dry land.” It was made dry land but was named earth, just as this firmament was made but was named heaven. So when the waters had been separated, the dry land came forth looking like sodden ground, for the waters had only just withdrawn. Once the earth was laid bare, the Creator commands: “Let the earth bring forth green plants, yielding seed according to kind and according to likeness, and the fruit tree whose seed is in it according to kind and according to likeness.” Not even this shames the heretics. Plants and trees and grass beget according to likeness, and did God beget something unlike himself? And again, when the four-footed animals, the creeping things and the birds came to be, God says: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things that have living souls, and winged creatures flying over the earth, according to kind.” Wild beasts, creeping things, birds, swimming creatures, plants, grass and trees all beget according to kind and according to likeness, and did God alone beget something unlike himself? And when God was fashioning us, he said: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness.” Is the work made according to likeness, while the craftsman is unlike?

But notice something remarkable. Heretical malice often finds itself a lair. “If you say,” they reply, “that the Son is according to likeness in the same way that we are, we accept it.” But likeness by nature is one thing, and likeness by grace another. We are according to the likeness; he is the likeness. For “whoever has seen me has seen the Father,” whereas we are only according to the likeness. The servants of God must inquire into the differences between words. God says: “Let the earth sprout green plants and the fruit tree bearing fruit.” Then he says: “Let the earth bring forth four-footed animals and wild beasts.” Why “let it sprout” there, and “let it bring forth” here? Shoots and trees and fruits sprout every year. Since the waters were to remain in the earth and these things were always to come forth from it, he says “let it sprout.” But for the animals he says “let it bring forth,” because once they had been born from the earth, they would no longer be born from the earth again, but from their own succession of offspring. And it was so. The word ran into deed, and the earth was adorned. It remained for the heaven to be adorned as well.

Why does he make the adornment of the earth come before that of heaven? Because of the polytheistic error that was going to spring up about the sun, moon and stars. God said: “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven.” Why did he not make the sun and moon on the first day? Because the firmament in which they were to be fixed had not yet come into being. And not only for that reason, but also because there were not yet any fruits that needed warming. The fruits sprouted on the third day. And again, so that no one would think they sprouted by the nature of the sun, God made the sun, moon and stars only when the work of creation had been completed. From what did he make them? We have said that on the first day he made all things out of what did not exist, but on the other days out of what already existed. From what, then, did the sun come? From the light made on the first day, which the craftsman transformed as he willed and refashioned into different appearances: here the mass of light, there the stars. It is as if someone were to set out a lump of gold and then cut it into coins; that is how he arranged the ordering of light. Just as he divided the abyss, which was then a single body of water, into seas, rivers, springs, lakes and wells, so too the craftsman cut up the light, which was one and uniform, and divided it into sun and moon and stars. I want to inquire how God made the lights. He appears to have made them outside heaven and then fixed them up above. Just as a craftsman, once he has finished a picture, then fixes it on a wall, so God first made the lights outside heaven and then fixed them up above, like a craftsman. Scripture testifies to this: “And God made the two lights, and set them in the heaven.” How, then, did he fix them? Were the two fixed in the same place? That makes no sense. What then? They were fixed in accordance with God’s own word. God set the lights, it says, “the great light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night.” When the sun was fixed in the east, the moon was fixed in the west, since she was commanded to rule the night and he the day. So the moon came into being, and on her first day she is born full. The work was not to be mutilated from the start; the light had to be displayed just as it was made. Afterward, by her changes, she marked out times and seasons and the differences between days. So God makes her full, as though on her fifteenth day. The sun rose at dawn; and since the moon was fixed at dawn, she appeared toward the west. Then, as the sun ran his own course toward the west, the moon at once began to rise, so that the words “let them rule the day and the night” might be fulfilled.

Next question: why did God make the moon full? Pay attention, for the thought is deep. Since she was made on the fourth day, she ought to have appeared four days old. But then again, if she had been four days old, she would not have held out to the far end of the west. So she was found to be eleven days ahead. She was four days old and appeared fifteen days old. So the moon was eleven days ahead of the sun, not in her making but in her shining. For this reason she pays back to the sun the days she gained on him then. For the lunar reckoning, counting each month as twenty-nine and a half days, makes three hundred and fifty-four days in the twelve months of the year. If you reckon the month this way, at twenty-nine and a half days, the days of the year come to three hundred and fifty-four, so that each year the moon pays back to the sun the days she gained then. Let whoever is good at reckoning work it out.

“Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth.” Since the nature of fire was to rise upward, God put a bridle on that nature, so that it should send its radiance not upward but downward. Fire cannot bear to turn downward, only upward. If you have a torch, turn it downward, and you will see that even when you turn the torch, the fire runs upward. So, since he knew its nature was such, he bound it, so that it would shine not according to its nature but according to his command. Some of you may have watched oil running from a lamp, how the fire is dragged down along with the oil: the force of the oil pulls it downward while the nature of the fire runs upward, and it cries out as though suffering violence. Whenever fire is forced to run against its natural course, it gives off a sound like something suffering violence, like something travelling against nature. Whenever something contrary to nature happens to an element, it cries out. Why? When oil is poured on fire, it makes no sound; but if water is poured on it, it crackles. Both are liquids. But oil is a food that comes from a tree, the olive is nourishing, and fire is always friendly to wood, so it gladly receives what comes from its kin. But if water is poured on fire, it crackles, because it is fighting its opposite. Fire belongs to the air, for they are akin. You blow on a lamp, the air turns the fire to smoke, and it is found nowhere, because it has run off to its kin. See the craftsman’s wisdom; see his power. He set the lights in heaven to shine upon the earth. “And let them be,” it says, “for signs and for days and for years.”

What does “for signs” mean? The idle talkers have poured out their hopes on astrology, reading signs of things that have no reality. Isaiah testifies that nothing can be read from the stars about human life, when he says: “Let the astrologers of heaven stand up, and those who look at the signs, and let them tell you what is going to happen.” So heaven gives no sign about human life. Do you want to learn what its signs are? It signals rains, winds, storms and fair weather. The stars signal these things, and they do so because of God’s love for humankind, so that the sailor may see the sign and escape danger, and the farmer may catch the scent of winter and plough his land in good time. There is also a sign of war and of peace. The Saviour confirmed these signs, which are simple and free of meddling curiosity. For he says to the Jews: “Hypocrites, if you see a cloud rising from the west, you say, ‘A storm is coming,’ and so it happens. And if you see the sky red in the evening, you say, ‘Fair weather,’ and there is fair weather. And if you see the sky gloomy in the evening, you say, ‘A storm is coming.’” And then he adds: “You know how to judge the face of heaven and earth, but you do not know this time?” These are the signs that are safe to observe: summer, winter, rain, fair weather. These are not foreign to piety, and they belong to God. One could go on at length about astrology. But that would require a strong voice and an instrument that does not falter. The mind keeps pace with speech, and reasoning grows weak along with the tongue. So let us move on to simpler matters. “Let them be for signs and for seasons.” A period of time is one thing and a season another. Time is duration; a season is the opportune moment. No one says, “It is the period for gathering grapes.” No one says, “It is the period for marrying the maiden,” but rather, “It is the season to marry the maiden,” “the season for sowing,” and “the season for harvest.” And Solomon says: “A season to give birth and a season to die, a season to build and a season to tear down.” By “season” he means the opportune moment. The stars signal this: for example, the rising of the Pleiades marks the beginning of harvest, and the setting of the Pleiades the beginning of sowing. These things are foreign to impiety and belong to piety. The feasts of God are also called seasons. God says: “Three seasons in the year you shall keep a feast to me: the feast of Unleavened Bread, the feast of Pentecost, the feast of Tabernacles.” Three seasons. There you have signs and seasons. Again, the moon produces the days, with reference to the sabbath, and the months. The sun keeps the turning points of the years: spring, the equinox, summer and autumn. These laws stand unshaken. He spoke, and they were fixed; he commanded, and they were founded. Now turn your mind to this. Who is the craftsman of these things? Who made them? The Father? No one disputes that. The Son? The heretics agree to this too, but not rightly. For they say that the Father made the Son, and the Son made all things. Am I to accept this impiety? Since it ties up the heretics’ reasoning in unbreakable bonds, let us ask the prophets whether the one who made all things has anyone greater than himself, or whether he is higher than all. For they fall by their own premise.

They say that the Son made all things, but that the Father made him. May God be merciful to us for repeating the blasphemy! For truly it is a horror to repeat the words of the ungodly. Yet we imitate the physicians, who thrust their hands into wounds to cleanse the sores; so the apostle too was compelled to mention shameful things, not to defile his tongue but to cleanse away sins. They say that the Son made all things, but that the Father made him. I will ask the prophets: Who is it that made heaven, and what kind of being is he? The prophet Isaiah says: "Thus says the Lord, who made heaven and fixed it, who established the earth and what is in it, who gives breath to the people upon it and spirit to those who walk on it: I am the Lord. Before me there is no god, and after me there is no god. I am, and there is no other." These are the words of the one who made heaven and earth: the Only-begotten, who according to the heretics came into being and only then created. But the sinner is caught in the words of his own lips. Blessed Jeremiah says: "Thus shall you say." To whom? To the Greeks. "Let the gods who did not make heaven and earth perish from the earth. The Lord, who made heaven by his understanding, he is the living and true God." If the God who made heaven is true, and the heretics themselves confess that the Son is the one who made heaven and earth, what conflict is there when Christ says, "That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent"? When the Savior said these things, whether through the prophets or in his own person, he did not say "That they may know you, the only God" to set the Father against himself, but to distinguish him from the falsely named gods. That is why Paul too says: "You turned from idols to serve a living and true God." He calls him true to refute the falsely named gods, and living to expose the dead idols. For my part I think, or rather I believe, that the dead are indignant with us when they hear us call the idols dead. "You insult our rank," they say. "We who once lived are called dead; why are those that never lived called dead?" "Let the gods who did not make heaven and earth perish. The Lord, who made the heavens by his understanding, he is the living and true God." Who is the living one? The one who made heaven. Do the heretics' definitions still stand? Does their impiety not fall? Is not true religion proven? Is not their mischief undone? You cannot grasp the works of the Maker, and yet you pry into the Craftsman and try to track him down? What does David cry out? "How great are your works, O Lord! In wisdom you have made them all." The prophets magnify the works; the heretics belittle the Craftsman. He is great in counsel and mighty in his works, he who fixed the heaven out of waters. For I cannot leave this wonder behind. It was congealed out of waters, and it bears water; it was made solid from waters, and it carries the abyss. And yet this [?] wonder, I say, is not without an example. Have you seen sheets of ice borne up on water and carrying snow on top? Winter made them. Does God not make such things? He did not make heaven as a sphere, as the vain talkers philosophize. For he did not make a revolving sphere; rather, as the prophet says (and how then does the sun run?): "He who roofed the heaven like a vault and stretched it out like a tent." None of us is so impious as to be persuaded by the vain talkers. The prophets say that heaven has a beginning and an end. That is why the sun does not go up but goes out. Scripture says: "The sun went out over the earth, and Lot entered Zoar." So it is clear that according to Scripture the sun went out and did not go up. And again it says, "Its going out is from the end of heaven"—its going out, not its going up. If heaven is a sphere, it has no end. For where does something that is round on every side have an end? Is it David alone who says this, or the Savior as well? Hear him saying: "When the Son of Man comes in his glory, he will send out his angels with a trumpet and a great voice, and they will gather his elect from one end of heaven to the other."

Now we ask where the sun sets and where it runs during the night. According to those outside, it runs under the earth. But what do we say, who call heaven a tent? Pay attention, I beg you, and see whether the statement is false. If you hold a seal attested by the truth, the facts of place agree with the words. Imagine a vault set over us. According to this figure, the east is there, the north here, the south there, the west there. When the sun has risen and is about to set, it does not set under the earth. Instead, going out at the ends of heaven, it runs to the northern parts, hidden as though behind a wall, since the waters do not allow its course to be seen; it runs through the northern parts and reaches the east. And how is this made clear? Blessed Solomon says in Ecclesiastes (and this is an attested scripture, not a rejected one): "The sun rises, and the sun sets. Rising, it goes to the west and circles toward the north; circling round and round, it rises in its own place." Learn from the state of things in winter that it runs toward the south and circles the north. For then it does not rise from the middle of the east but slants toward the southern region, and cutting across a short distance it makes a short day. Then, after setting and running its circuit again, it makes a long night. We know, brothers, that the sun does not always come forth from the same point. How then do the days become short? Its rising draws near to the southern region. Then, instead of taking the high road, it cuts short the slanting one and makes the days short. And having set at the far end of the west, it must circle through the night the whole west, the whole north and the whole east, and reach the far end of the south; and so the night must be long. When, however, the lengths are equal and its stride is equal, it makes the equinox. Again, leaning toward the north as in winter it leaned toward the south, and climbing to the far parts of the north, it is raised high and makes the day long; and having only a small circuit to run, it makes the night short. It was not the children of the Greeks who taught us these things. They do not even want this; they say that the stars and the sun run under the earth. But our Scripture, the divine teacher—Scripture instructs and enlightens us. Then he made the sun an unfailing light, and the moon, which puts on its beauty and puts it off and clothes itself in it again. The work shows the craftsman. The craftsman never fails; the work endures. For the light of the moon is not used up but hidden. And it also becomes an image of us mortal human beings. Consider how many ages it has been rising. And yet when it is new we say, "Today the moon is born." Why? Because it is an image of our bodies. It is born, it grows, it becomes full, it diminishes, it wanes, it sets; for we too are born, we grow, we reach our fullness, we pass our prime, we decline, we grow old, we die, we set. But it is born again, because we too shall rise, and another birth awaits us. That is why the Savior, wishing to show that as we were born here so we are born again, says: "When the Son of Man comes in the regeneration." The moon is a pledge of the resurrection. "You see me," it says, "hidden and then appearing again, and do you give up your hopes?" Was not the sun made for us? The moon for us? All created things? What is there that is not a pledge of our resurrection? Is not night an image of death? Bodies lie cast down in the darkness; you cannot make out their forms. Often you feel the faces of sleepers with your hand and do not know which face is this person's and which is that one's; so you ask, that a voice may announce who is hidden in the darkness. Just as night covers our forms, so that even if we are all in the same place no one recognizes anyone else, so death comes and dissolves our forms, so that no one recognizes anyone. You pass by tombs. If you see many skulls in a grave, do you know whose this one is? But the one who fashioned them knows; the one who dissolved them understands where these forms came from. Do you not marvel at God's handiwork? Among so many forms in so many tens of thousands there is no likeness. Even if you run to the ends of the world, you will find no one exactly alike; and even if you do, they will differ in the nose or the eye, so that what is distinct may appear. Twins come out of one womb, and still the likeness is broken.

Will he, then, who brought so many forms into being from nothing be unable to renew them after he has dissolved them? Do not, like a wretched man, measure God's power and God's wisdom by your own reasonings. Do not suppose that God can do only as much as you can reckon. If he can do only as much as I conceive, then, I dare to say, God is very small, for my mind has measured him. But if he surpasses thought and overcomes reasoning, then the Maker is unsearchable and his works beyond comprehension. Let the heretics be questioned from visible things, so that they may learn how helpless they are. Since God said, "Let there be a firmament," and at once the Word carried it out, he has left us this pledge that he himself made it. Today we leave the sky bare in the evening, and rising suddenly we find another firmament congealed out of the clouds. These are partial pledges of those first works, when you see the sky darkened and another firmament made out of the clouds. He who now makes clouds so swiftly shows how swiftly he made heaven then. And what does he do? How do the clouds rain? He made the clouds like wineskins, and through them he draws up the waters of the sea, which are salty, fills the clouds, changes the water, and waters the earth. Let them tell us how the weight is carried up on high, how it is drawn up, how the clouds are drawn full. They do not empty at once but travel a long way, wherever the Master commands; and God's command is like a bond laid on the clouds, not allowing them to rain until he gives the nod. That they are wineskins David testifies: "He gathers the waters of the sea as in a wineskin." And see the marvel. He gathers the waters; the immortal, invisible hand lies upon them and does not let them empty all at once, but little by little. Just as a woman spinning a fine thread divides the wool into many different strands, so he divides the boundless depth of the sea into drops, shaping it as it were, and so sends it to the earth. But here is the marvel: if it has been untied, how is it not quickly emptied? If it is tied, why does it flow? You have an example—a weak one, but able to convince you. Have you seen a water-catcher? Have you seen how it is pierced with holes at the bottom? When something lies over the top, it holds its load, and it is stopped up below because of what lies on top. So the immortal finger of God lies upon the clouds, releasing as much as he wills and holding back as much as he wills, so that he may send the gift over all the earth. He does this especially in the late rains, when he drenches the whole earth, watering now this region and now another. That is why the prophet says: "And he will rain on one city, and on another city he will not rain. One portion will be rained on, and the portion on which he does not rain will dry up." Yet what lies upon the clouds is not God's finger but a command [?]; I have shaped the account after our own manner. He commands, and they do not rain. Scripture says this too: "I will command the clouds not to rain rain." For "how great are your works, O Lord! In wisdom you have made them all." Have you seen God's handiwork? Have you seen how it stops the mouths of the heretics, who do not understand creation and yet busy themselves prying into the Creator? All things obey God's law. Heaven stands, not upheld by its own power but made firm by divine law. For when I am at a loss as to how heaven was congealed out of waters, blessed David resolves my perplexity, saying: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm." Why "made firm"? Because they came from waters. What is already firm is never said to have been made firm; no one can say, "The rock was made firm." To be made firm is one thing; to be firm is another. Something is said to be made firm when what was loose and slack is solidified. That is why Peter, when he raised up the paralyzed man, says: "Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we had made him walk? The God of our fathers, the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, has glorified his servant Jesus; and by faith in his name, his name has made firm this man whom you see and know." He made the paralyzed man firm. That is why "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm." Out of loose and scattered waters, by the word of the Lord, the clouds are lifted on high. Look, I beg you. The bitter water is changed: the clouds draw it from the sea, and what was drawn up bitter from the deep they make sweet and fit to drink. Christ has raised us from the depths, and yet we do not put away our bitterness.

Who is it that made heaven and earth? I say that it is Christ. And how do I know this? Because if he were not Master of all things, he would not in the Gospel have worked his miracles through every part of creation. For he worked them through all the elements—through earth, through sea, through air, through fire—so that he might be shown to be Master of all created things. The light of evening has now come in upon the light of day. The sun is shining and the lamp is being lit: the end of day and the prelude to night. But you, when you see the lamp and the sun, say: "Yours is the day, and yours is the night; you prepared the light and the sun." But the lighting of the lamps does not interrupt our discourse. For the sun must run at his command. "For the sun knew its setting," so that it might be shown that Christ is Master of all his works. John proclaims this: "All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being that has come into being." But he had to shine forth not only in word but also in deed. He says to the sea, "Be silent, be still," and it was stilled, and the work recognized its Craftsman. For he spoke to the sea, and it fell silent; he spoke to the wind, and it was stilled. If it had not obeyed, he would not have been its Maker. If he were not Master of water, he would not have changed water into wine. If he were not Master of heaven, a star from heaven would not have proclaimed him. If he were not Master of the sun, the sun would not have clothed itself in darkness at the cross. Christ is on the cross, and the sun is darkened. What a wonder! Creation itself could not bear the outrage done to its Master. The sun was darkened, so that you might learn that even on the cross he was Master of the sun. The earth was shaken, so that you might learn that it was of him that David said: "He who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble." The rocks were split, so that you might learn of whom the prophet spoke: "His wrath melts rulers, and the rocks were shattered by him." The tombs were opened, so that the resurrection might appear and God who raises the dead might shine forth through all things.

But we must also offer a moral discourse. The lamp calls us to say: "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths." Evening has come, so that we may say: "Let my prayer rise like incense before you, the lifting up of my hands like an evening sacrifice." And why not a morning one? Pay attention here. For we ought to understand what we sing; David says, "Sing with understanding." "The lifting up of my hands like an evening sacrifice." Moses—or rather God—ordered two sacrifices to be offered, one in the morning and one in the evening. The morning sacrifice was a thanksgiving for the night, for the one who has been kept safe through the night gives thanks in the day. The evening sacrifice was a thanksgiving for the day: "Since you have kept me through the day," it says, "I thank you for the whole day." The morning sacrifice does not accept one who has sinned in the night. That is why he says, "The lifting up of my hands like an evening sacrifice." You come to the evening and spread out your hands. If they have boldness, let them be spread out. If they have not written injustice, if they have not robbed the poor, if they have not defrauded orphans, let them be lifted up as hands that can look God in the face. "The lifting up of my hands" means "See, Lord, my hands are clean." For just as one who has sinned cannot lift up his face but is bowed down by his conscience, so a defiled hand does not even dare to come before God's face. Look: if your hands are clean of injustice, let them be spread out. That is why the patriarch Abraham refused to take gain from shameful profit when the king of Sodom said to him, "Take everything; only release the women." So that he might have boldness, he took nothing; and having clean hands he said, "I will stretch out my hands to God, who made heaven and earth." And he stretched them out, since they were not defiled by unjust gain. "The lifting up of my hands." Paul explains "the lifting up of my hands": "I desire, then, that in every place the men should pray, lifting up holy hands without anger or quarreling." The evening demands of us the works of the evening. You spread out your hands, and the Craftsman examines them. The morning hour comes, and if your hand or your mind is not clean, you do not even dare to look upon the morning hour. Experience is the teacher. Consider how someone who has remained pure enters with boldness, as though walking in his own courtyard. For chastity in the night gives him boldness in the morning hour. That is why David says: "If I remembered you upon my bed, at dawn I meditated on you." I thank God. I remember that when my voice was failing, the word of God restored it, looking not to our worth but to your longing. Let us pray, then, in truth of heart, that we may have peace, speak boldly at dawn, flee the madness of heresy, pursue the orthodox faith, and send up glory to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
